The equation governing the time-evolution of a probability distribution in a system with random variations has a dual interpretation as a time-dependent wavefunction in a related quantum system with variable magnetic field strength. This classical-quantum equivalence implies a correspondence between the solutions to the equations describing random variations and quantum behavior, and we demonstrate this principle in the context of non-stationary conditions and solvent effects. Furthermore, the same classical-quantum equivalence allows for a more intuitive understanding of how probability distribution peaks and troughs correspond to the locations of wavefunction density peaks and troughs in the associated quantum system. This classical-quantum duality is utilized to analyze quantum behavior in systems with variable magnetic field strength. Specifically, the effect of quantum tunneling in such systems can be understood in terms of classical probability barriers, while quantum oscillations can be induced by periodically varying the magnetic field strength. This approach is applied to a study of quantum oscillations in superconducting qubits, and further discussed in the context of quantum heat transfer and dissipation. This research highlights the potential benefits of viewing quantum behavior as the time-reversal-invariant evolution of a probability distribution, and the potential for using quantum oscillations as a means of controlling dissipation. This approach is anticipated to have a range of applications in the design of novel quantum devices, including those based on superconducting, semiconductor, and atomic systems. Entity linking, the task of identifying and disambiguating mentions of
entities in unstructured text, is a crucial component of natural language
processing. To improve the accuracy of this process, particularly when dealing
with unknown or out-of-vocabulary entities, is a significant challenge. Current
datasets for entity linking, such as Wikidata100, Wikipedia Graph and
WikiLinks, primarily focus on articles within the English Wikipedia. To create a
more comprehensive test bed for entity linking, we have developed the WikiGUM
dataset, a large-scale collection of entity mentions extracted from the
Google Knowledge Graph Search results, which are then linked to their respective
Wikidata IDs. This dataset is built upon a 100K Wikipedia document corpus and
includes over 1.2M entities, 13M entity mentions, and 42M entity-link pairs.
Compared to previous entity linking datasets, WikiGUM presents distinct
challenges due to its diverse and high-quality entities, which exhibit a wide
range of language and topic variations. To our knowledge, WikiGUM is the largest
entity linked corpus available. To showcase the utility of WikiGUM, we have
conducted baseline experiments on entity linking, and our results indicate that
it is a highly challenging but valuable resource for entity linked research. As
such, WikiGUM is expected to inspire future entity linked studies. WikiGUM is
publicly available for research and development purposes. To access WikiGUM,
please visit our project's website at https://wikigum.github.io/. We welcome any
further use or contributions to enhance WikiGUM's utility. We invite the research
community to participate in advancing the state-of-the-art in entity linked research.

A crucial component of autonomous vehicles' local navigation, loop closure detection, is critical due to its ability to significantly decrease navigation errors. Most existing loop closure methods rely on forward or backward propagation of features, which are influenced by the dynamic environment and vehicle pose. This study presents a novel bi-directional loop closure approach, leveraging the vehicle's historical path to efficiently identify loops, and incorporates a feature propagation mechanism to isolate local environmental features, preserving the representation of the road layout. The proposed method achieves improved detection accuracy, outperforming single-direction propagation and forward propagation by 27.9% and 24.2% on the KITTI dataset, and operates efficiently with minimal computational resources, making it suitable for real-time implementation on various hardware platforms. Recent advancements in unsupervised reinforcement learning have led to the development of agents capable of learning from minimal task-specific supervision. To build upon these advancements, we have created a new framework called Hierarchical World Model for Unsupervised Reinforcement Learning (HiWML), which enables RL agents to acquire knowledge from their environment without explicit supervision. HiWML is composed of two distinct components: the World Model Learning Agent and the Task Adaptation Agent. The World Model Learning Agent enables agents to learn low-level skills within their environment, while the Task Adaptation Agent allows them to learn high-level abstractions for new, unseen tasks. HiWML is capable of producing a hierarchical world model, which is used to train a policy that can be applied to various tasks without explicit supervision. To evaluate the effectiveness of HiWML, we have tested it on multiple complex control tasks, resulting in superior performance compared to state-of-the-art methods, especially in situations with limited task-specific demonstrations. HiWML has the potential to be applied to a wide range of unsupervised RL tasks, including autonomous driving, robotic manipulation, and video game training. We provide an explicit formula for the Weierstrass sigma function using a derivative of a Jacobi theta function. The proof leverages a key equation obtained from a Berry-Atiyah equation applied to a specific curve obtained from the Weierstrass p-form. A corresponding Berry curvature tensor is defined via a 2-by-2 matrix constructed from the period matrix of the Weierstrass p-form. In addition, we offer two equivalent definitions for the Berry curvature, both of which ultimately lead to the given explicit formula for the Weierstrass sigma function. Furthermore, we establish that the Berry curvature tensor is non-degenerate, and provide explicit expressions for its inverse and the Weierstrass zeta function. Lastly, we demonstrate that the Weierstrass phi function and epsilon function can be expressed in terms of the Weierstrass sigma function and its logarithmic derivatives. The interaction between high-velocity clouds and the surrounding halo gas is a significant factor in the acceleration of cosmic rays. A theoretical model describing this interaction is proposed, taking into account the impact of magnetic fields. A key characteristic of the model is the use of a constant radial velocity, which is supported by observations of the G135 and SgrB2 clouds. A comparison of the model's predictions to observations of the Orion Molecular Cloud reveals that the acceleration of cosmic rays is influenced by the magnetic field's polarization angle. The results suggest that the magnetic field's polarization angle plays a crucial role in the acceleration of cosmic rays. Recent breakthroughs in self-supervised learning have enabled the development of highly accurate representations without relying on expensive and limited annotated data. This research examines the internal structure of these learned representations by analyzing the distribution of their representation vectors in high-dimensional space. Our study reveals that the manifolds of these self-supervised and fully supervised representations exhibit distinct properties, with the former displaying a smoother structure and tighter clustering of its representation points. To gain a deeper understanding of these complex representation manifolds, we propose a novel method for approximating their local linear tangent spaces at specific representation vectors. Our approach, which relies on the optimal transport metric, demonstrates the practical feasibility of applying this method to complex representation manifolds and further reveals that the tangent spaces at these points are highly orthogonal to the normal vectors of their respective manifolds. Our analysis also sheds light on the effectiveness of the contrastive learning approach by examining how its use affects the local geometry of the representation manifold. Our study provides valuable insights into the internal structure of these complex representation manifolds, which are crucial for advancing representation learning research. Our findings are expected to serve as a valuable resource for advancing representation learning research and can be used to inform the design of more effective self-supervised learning techniques. Additionally, the proposed estimator outperforms existing nonlinear algorithms, as evident from the experimental comparisons. The proposed teleoperation framework is expected to contribute to the development of more precise and reliable teleoperation systems. This research introduces a method for determining the robustness of structural systems. It involves using existing limit load analysis techniques to establish a range of loads that a structure can support, while also accounting for the variability in material strength. By combining this approach with a reliability assessment method, the study calculates the expected minimum load that a structure can handle, considering the uncertainty in material strength. To achieve this, the study utilizes a sampling-based reliability estimation method, which provides an approximate measure of the critical load. Bird classification from images is a complex task due to significant differences in size and diversity. To overcome this, we utilize transfer learning with pre-trained deep learning models, combining low and high-level visual features. Our approach specifically highlights the importance of color in bird classification and leverages spatial awareness to improve classification. We evaluate the effectiveness of various techniques, including data augmentation, image filtering, and artificial neural networks, to identify the most effective methods for bird classification. Our experiments utilizing the 2019 Bird Species Classification Competition dataset show that a combination of spatial pooling and color extraction, integrated with a deep learning model, yields a high accuracy of 87.6%. This approach also demonstrates generalizability by successfully classifying novel bird images not included in the training set. We also explore the potential of using self-supervised learning for bird classification and find it to be a promising direction for further research. In the realm of generative models, specifically in the field of Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs), mode collapse is a significant challenge that occurs during training. Mode collapse occurs when a GAN model generates the same output from a single input sample, essentially failing to produce diverse outputs. To address this issue, this paper introduces an innovative method that utilizes the concept of deep invertible functions to enhance the diversity of GAN mode coverage. By employing deep invertible functions to learn the inverse mapping of feature space, this method effectively enables the GAN model to produce a more diverse range of outputs from a single input. Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of this proposed approach in mitigating mode collapse and improving output diversity. Additionally, this method offers the added benefit of fast training speed and efficient computation. To validate the performance of this proposed approach, experiments were conducted using the CIFAR-10 and MNIST datasets, with the MNIST dataset exhibiting notable improvements in diverse mode coverage. Lastly, this paper explores the broader implications of this proposed approach in the context of future research directions. In the absence of exotic matter with non-conventional energy conditions, diverse cosmological models have been found to evolve towards a singular Big Bang in a wide array of spacetime geometries, including static spacetimes in imaginary scalar-flux space. This phenomenon has been attributed to the presence of a complex, effective cosmological constant, which arises from the compactification of spacetime along the imaginary coordinate. Notably, the complex constant exhibits a non-trivial dependence on the compactification radius, whereas the scalar-flux modulates its sign, thereby influencing the nature of the singularity - whether it's a Big Bang or Big Crunch. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the cosmological models can be extended to include a Minkowski spacetime in the absence of the scalar-flux. This extension is achieved by embedding the model in a higher-dimensional spacetime with an odd number of dimensions, where the complex constant and scalar-flux are the compactified coordinates. A significant amount of research has been conducted on image dehazing methods, 
and the dehazed images obtained still differ in quality based on the used 
algorithm. To address this issue, we focus on developing a new metric for 
evaluating the dehazed images themselves. Our proposed metric relies on three 
key groups of features: spatial, frequency, and spatial-frequency-based features. 
By combining these features using optimal weighting, our metric can be calculated 
as a weighted sum. To test its effectiveness, we have applied it to a large dataset 
of both indoor and outdoor images with varying levels of haze, and the results show 
its potential. Furthermore, we have compared it to state-of-the-art metrics for image 
dehazing using both subjective and objective assessments. Our results indicate that our 
metric performs better than existing ones in assessing the dehazed images. To make 
our metric more practical, we have developed a new database of dehazed images with 
ground-truth dehazing levels, and we will make it available to the research community. 
Finally, we have developed a new dehazing level map prediction network called the 
Local Patch Attention Convolutional Neural Network (LP-ACNN), which can be used to 
improve the dehazing methods themselves. Our proposed metric, database, and LP-ACNN 
are expected to contribute to the advancement of future research in this field. To our 
knowledge, this work represents a pioneering effort in developing a comprehensive 
framework for image dehazing using deep learning methods. Our research code and models 
will be made publicly available for others to use and build upon. To see more results, 
please visit our project page at https://sites.google.com/view/dehaze-level-map/.

and Machine Intelligence (TPAMI) journal. To see the corresponding journal version,

Learning from datasets consisting of positive and unlabeled examples without class labels is a significant challenge, especially in real-world applications where data is often severely unbalanced. Existing solutions to this problem often come with drawbacks, such as the need for parameter adjustment or the assumption of a known positive class distribution. In contrast, this study proposes a novel and efficient semi-supervised learning method that addresses these issues by leveraging the availability of positive and unlabeled data, as well as partially labeled data, to learn class boundaries without requiring parameter adjustment. We introduce a new metric, the Fuzzy K-nearest neighbor ratio (FKNR), which effectively captures local density variations and uses it to develop a FKNR-based classifier. We further introduce a novel loss function that utilizes the FKNR to learn the local density gradient, ultimately enabling the model to learn from positive and unlabeled data, as well as partially labeled data, without requiring parameter adjustment. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in handling unbalanced data, and we show that our approach outperforms existing methods in both parameter-adjustment-free and parameter-adjusted settings. However, when all segments are already connected in a simple polygon, the problem becomes straightforward and can be solved in O(n log n) time using a sweep-line algorithm. By leveraging this observation, a modified algorithm has been devised that efficiently finds a minimal set of segments needed to transform any polygonal chain into a simple polygon, thus resolving the Polygonation Problem in O(n log n) time. Additionally, a related variant of the problem, referred to as the Polygonation Deletion Problem, involves identifying the minimum set of segments necessary to remove in order to transform a polygonal chain into a simple polygon, and this problem can also be solved in O(n log n) time using a modified algorithm inspired by the Polygonation Problem solution. Both algorithms have been implemented using the sweep-line method, and experimental results confirm their efficiency and performance. It has been established that both problems are NP-hard, and several related problems have been shown to be NP-complete as well. Furthermore, when restricted to specific types of polygonal chains such as polygonal paths and polygonal chains without self-intersections, several related problems were found to be NP-complete. However, when all segments are already non-intersecting, a simpler approach has been devised that can solve the Polygonation Problem in O(n log n) time using a sweep-line algorithm. It has also been established that a related problem known as the Polygonation Transformation Problem, which deals with transforming a polygonal chain into a simple polygon by adding or deleting segments, is solvable in O(n^2 log n) time using a combination of dynamic programming and a greedy approach. When restricted to non-overlapping segments, a related problem known as the Polygonation Deletion Deletion Problem, which deals with identifying the deletion of segments necessary to transform a polygonal chain into a simple polygon, can also be solved in O(n^2 log n) time using a combination of dynamic programming and a greedy approach. All these results have been proven to be tight. Finally, a related problem known as the Polygonation Deletion Transformation Problem, which deals with transforming a polygonal chain into a simple polygon by adding or deleting segments, can also be solved in O(n^2 log n) time using a combination of dynamic programming and a greedy approach. A cloud-radio access network (C-RAN) is a flexible technology that enables the efficient management of massive multiple-input multiple-output systems. By moving base station functions to a centralized cloud, C-RAN offers improved interference mitigation and increased downlink data rates. In this research, we demonstrate that C-RAN can benefit from a learning-based approach to optimize its performance. A novel system is presented where a central cloud station utilizes a reinforcement learning algorithm to minimize total transmission power while satisfying downlink data rate requirements for all users. Initially, we establish that this system can be optimized to achieve an optimal outcome using a traditional optimization method. We then develop an actor-critic reinforcement learning approach to achieve this optimal outcome, and our simulation results confirm that this approach enables the C-RAN system to converge to the optimal solution efficiently. By comparing the performance of the learning-based system to a conventional C-RAN system, our results show that the learning-based approach can offer significant performance improvements, including faster system convergence and lower power consumption. Notably, our simulations indicate that the learning-based approach can achieve substantial gains of up to 15% and 30% in terms of data rates and power consumption, respectively, compared to the conventional C-RAN system. These findings suggest that machine learning can be a valuable tool for enhancing the performance of massive MIMO systems. We believe that this work will pave the way for future research on the integration of machine learning techniques in C-RAN systems. We also propose the possibility of extending this research to other advanced MIMO technologies, such as non-orthogonal multiple access and network MIMO. This paper explores the challenge of merging predictors, a fundamental concept in machine learning, by formalizing it as a multi-armed bandit problem. Our primary objective is to balance the performance of individual predictors while minimizing misalignment between them and the target learning task. We propose a novel algorithm, known as Adaptive Predictive Alignment, that effectively navigates this trade-off. Furthermore, our analysis confirms that A-PA algorithm achieves optimal results, as it cannot be surpassed by any other algorithm under the same conditions. Specifically, its performance is bound by the performance of the ideal combination of predictors, as measured by the regret ratio. To demonstrate the practical applications of our work, we conduct experiments on both synthetic and real-world data sets. The results show that A-PA significantly outperforms existing methods in terms of reducing bias and achieving better overall performance. Secure end-to-end encryption has become a standard for online messaging, yet existing solutions often struggle to effectively address suspicious or malicious messages. To address these issues, we developed Wink, a custom-built, partially covert messaging system designed to allow recipients to verify the authenticity of incoming messages without appearing to react suspiciously. By leveraging the principles of plausibly deniable cryptography, Wink enables recipients to verify the authenticity of incoming messages without giving away their intentions, thereby facilitating a more secure process for both senders and recipients. Our experiments demonstrate that Wink successfully conceals the presence of suspicious messages within ordinary communication, as evidenced by the fact that ordinary messages and those containing suspicious intent are indistinguishable by machine learning algorithms. Furthermore, Wink allows recipients to reliably detect and respond to suspicious messages with minimal risk of detection, even when interacting with multiple such messages in quick succession. Overall, our results demonstrate that Wink effectively enables recipients to investigate potential security threats without compromising their own safety and privacy. The implementation and source code for Wink are available at https://github.com/kszheng/wink. We also provide a user-friendly web interface at https://messaging.csail.mit.edu/wink. The formal description of Wink's security properties is available in the appendix of this document. Additionally, we present a new method for detecting suspicious communication patterns, which we utilized in conjunction with real-world data from Signal and Telegram to develop a dataset of 10,000 suspicious messages. Our analysis reveals that our method is effective in identifying suspicious communication patterns, even within datasets that have been intentionally altered to include false positives. Our results are presented in detail in the companion paper "Detecting Suspicious Communication Patterns" at https://arxiv.org/doi/10.21276/fti.2022.11.18. Our research has been conducted in collaboration with Signal and the Signal Research Group, and we would like to express our gratitude to the Signal Foundation for their support. Finally, we discuss the potential for adapting Wink to integrate multiple secure protocols, thereby enhancing its overall security and reliability. Our work has been driven by the desire to address the pressing issue of online harassment and cyberbullying, which has become increasingly prevalent due to the COVID-19 pandemic. In remote sensing imaging systems, pan-sharpening plays a key role in enhancing the spatial resolution and detail of panchromatic images. A widely applied method, combining a pan image with a multi-spectral image of lower resolution, leverages the rich spectral details from the multi-spectral image to improve the resolution of the pan image. However, this approach often results in artifacts due to the misalignment between the two images caused by noise within the multi-spectral image. This paper presents an innovative pan-sharpening algorithm that utilizes the high-resolution panchromatic image to improve the multi-spectral image. The proposed method integrates a low-frequency image generated from the pan image with details extracted from the panchromatic image to produce a high-resolution multi-spectral image. A non-local self-similarity prior is incorporated to ensure smooth transitions between regions with different spectral details. Experimental results demonstrate the superior performance of the proposed method over existing ones on multiple datasets. Additionally, the algorithm has been successfully implemented on a smartphone device using a low-cost imaging sensor, showcasing its practical applicability. Expert gating is a crucial component in distributed models, allowing for efficient computation across multiple tasks. Current methods for expert gating often rely solely on the input data, resulting in computationally expensive inference processes. Autonomous vehicles rely heavily on precise localization techniques to perform effectively. Deep learning methods have gained traction recently for recognizing locations using 3D LiDAR data, yet these approaches face limitations in processing real-time data due to their computational complexity. This paper presents a novel, efficient technique for recognizing locations using 3D LiDAR data. By integrating a deep learning network, the proposed method extracts critical features from multi-view point cloud data in a real-time capable two-stream CNN architecture. This stream is initially pre-trained on a large-scale dataset, and then fine-tuned on a smaller dataset specific to the testing environment. By leveraging the pre-trained weights, the technique achieves significant computational reduction without compromising performance. Moreover, the proposed method implements a novel feature fusion technique, enabling it to extract essential geometric and structural features from the point cloud data. Extensive experiments demonstrate that this approach surpasses existing state-of-the-art methods in both accuracy and efficiency, achieving an impressive 81.3% accuracy under real-world conditions. This technique is also adaptable to various environments with minimal fine-tuning required, making it highly effective. A cutting-edge search for higgsinos at the LHC is described, focusing on the production of pairs with an energetic hard QCD jet, detectable via the presence of missing transverse energy and multiple high-mass jets. Data collected from the LHC at 13 TeV with integrated luminosity of 77.2 fb^-1 is analyzed. Signal events, featuring supersymmetric higgsinos that decay into neutralinos and gluinos, are compared to standard model backgrounds using advanced techniques in matrix element and neural network methods. Significantly improved signal detection is achieved through efficient categorization of signal events and targeted jet selection. This search yields no significant deviations from the standard model predictions. At a 95% confidence level, a maximum mass of 1.75 TeV is established for the higgsinos that decay into neutralinos, while masses of up to 1.87 TeV are set for the gluinos in the on-shell region. These findings significantly surpass previous limits set by the CMS collaboration. For supersymmetric models predicting the production of four jets and missing transverse energy, a 95% confidence level mass limit of 1.95 TeV is established. This search also provides improved exclusion mass limits for higgsinos and gluinos in a range of supersymmetric models, including those with compressed spectra. These results are the most stringent to date. This search also explores the potential of a multi-lepton search for the same supersymmetric models at high-luminosity LHC, revealing the potential for significant signal detection. We demonstrate that the extended version of a sub-additive convex function $f$ is also sub-additive convex. We find that the maximum $(d-2)$-leaky forcing number for the $d$-dimensional hypercube, $Q_d$, equals $2^d$ minus 2. To achieve this result, we first establish a lower bound on the $k$-leaky forcing number for the $k$-dimensional hypercube, yielding a value of at least $2^k-2$. By leveraging this finding, we demonstrate that the maximum $(d-2)$-leaky forcing number for the $d$-dimensional hypercube, $Q_d$, equals $2^d-2$. Notably, this result serves as a $(d-2)$-leaky analog to the established upper limit on the $k$-leaky forcing number for the $k$-dimensional hypercube, as detailed in the research of \cite{FHTW}. Our proof strategy involves the strategic selection of a specific hypercube vertex, followed by the application of the hypercube's inherent properties to derive the desired outcome. This study was motivated by the work of FHTW researchers, who defined the concept of $k$-leaky forcibility and demonstrated that the $d$-dimensional hypercube, $Q_d$, is $k$-leaky forcible with a forcing number of $2^d$. They also proposed the conjecture that the $d$-dimensional hypercube, $Q_d$, is $k$-leaky forcible with a forcing number of $2^k-1$. While we resolve this conjecture for the case where $k=d-2$, we leave the remaining cases unresolved for future investigation. Our research is complemented by the derivation of a lower bound on the $k$-leaky forcibility of the $d$-dimensional hypercube, yielding a value of at least $2^k-2$. Speedrunning has become a growing and dynamic gaming community that, unlike traditional players, focuses on achieving shortcuts and workarounds to reach goals in record time. This speedrunning approach differs from its conventional counterpart due to its emphasis on strategy and planning, particularly with the aid of pre-planned routes known as routes, which are developed by speedrunners to complete a game as quickly as possible. Machine listening tasks such as audio segmentation and sound event detection have a wide range of applications in smart homes, industrial settings, and social environments. Recent breakthroughs in deep neural networks have significantly improved performance when trained and tested within the same conditions. By incorporating adversarial domain transfer and knowledge distillation techniques, the model learns to adapt to new test datasets. Experimental results on the DCASE 2018 Task 1 dataset show that DASNet significantly outperforms the baseline model, achieving a 7.89% improvement in weighted F-score. Furthermore, the model's ability to achieve high performance in unseen environments while minimizing computational overhead has significant implications for real-world applications. Transformers have seen significant success in computer vision tasks, but their high computational cost limits their widespread application in real-time computer vision systems.  To address this, a new model called the Transformer-based Motion Refining Unit (T-MRU) has been developed for motion estimation, refining estimates at every frame.  T-MRU's design draws on the Transformer's ability to handle long-range relationships and its ability to handle varying input lengths, allowing it to effectively utilize the connections between multiple feature points.  T-MRU's efficiency is further enhanced through the use of residual blocks and the model's relatively small size.  As a result, T-MRU outperforms existing state-of-the-art motion estimation models, achieving superior accuracy while using significantly fewer FLOPs.  T-MRU's performance on multiple motion estimation tasks is demonstrated through extensive testing, and the model's source code has been made available for further research. This paper explores how the curvature changes when modifying the structure of space, particularly focusing on flat, intersecting plane surfaces. It demonstrates that increasing the curvature of specific, initially flat torus formations requires a non-standard expansion of the space, where either the local measurements shift in the opposite way across all the surfaces or all the surfaces intersect at distinct points. Furthermore, we establish that these configurations are the sole possibilities for creating such scenarios. Additionally, we prove that similar, more general flat formations exhibit the same behavior, where increasing the curvature necessitates a non-standard expansion of the space, resulting in local measurements that differ in the opposite way across all the codimension 1 submanifolds. Finally, we show that these configurations are the sole possibilities for creating such scenarios, even when considering more general flat formations with no inherent symmetry. In modern wireless communication systems, the efficiency of data transmission is often hindered by signal interference. A widely used technique for mitigating this issue is successive interference cancellation (SIC). Notwithstanding the effectiveness of SIC, the computational complexity involved in implementing it grows rapidly with the number of signals being decoded. The value function, a crucial concept, calculates the expected long-term reward resulting from taking a specific action at a given state. Despite its importance, the value function is often not directly applicable to multi-agent environments. To overcome this limitation, this paper introduces a concept called the \textit{global value function}, which represents the combined, discounted rewards experienced by all agents within the environment. The incorporation of the global value function enhances decision-making processes, especially in scenarios where multiple agents form alliances. The paper also proposes a new RL algorithm, called \textit{Global Value Function Iterated Policy Iteration} (GF-PIP), which utilizes the global value function to improve the policy. The algorithm iteratively updates the global value function and policy until convergence, using a combination of temporal difference and least squares methods. Theoretical analysis confirms the convergence of GF-PIP to an optimal policy. The algorithm's effectiveness is further demonstrated through simulation-based experiments on various multi-agent games, including the well-known public goods game and an adapted version of Starcraft. The results show that GF-PIP outperforms existing methods in achieving high returns. Additionally, the study reveals that GF-PIP can successfully improve cooperative policies in complex scenarios, such as competing with other agents or forming alliances. The algorithm's applicability is not limited to competitive games, as it can also improve policies in cooperative settings. The results highlight the significance of accounting for multi-agent interactions when designing RL algorithms. Theoretical models of brain function suggest that neurons are active only when they're needed, yet experimental evidence indicates that neurons fire randomly. Previous research has shown that a measure of variability called the moment activation (MA) can be used to mimic this pattern in idealized neurons. Our research demonstrates that MA can be an effective learning mechanism for artificial neural networks and even outperform traditional methods like backpropagation and reinforcement learning in certain tasks. Furthermore, MA can be used to learn from data that is not explicitly labeled, provided that the network is designed with an optimal architecture in relation to the underlying rules governing the data. Additionally, we found that MA can lead to the development of highly specialized neurons that continue to learn as the network learns new information. This research has significant implications for understanding how biological neural networks process information and for the design of more efficient artificial neural networks. Our findings also suggest that the brain's ability to learn from experience may rely on the activation of neurons rather than their overall activity level. We also found that MA can be used to model a type of neural disorder where the brain fails to learn from experience, provided that the brain's learning rules are based on the temporal relationships between different events. These findings provide new insights into the computational principles underlying brain function and can be used to inform the design of more biologically realistic artificial neural networks. This study delves into the concept of fairness within federated learning in distributed networks, where each client has its own data set. It highlights the challenges of simultaneously optimizing learning accuracy and fairness, especially in the context of data imbalance and heterogeneity. To address these issues, a novel approach using optimal transport theory is proposed, yielding two fairness-guaranteed algorithms. These algorithms, tested on real-world datasets, demonstrate the potential to achieve fairness without compromising learning accuracy. However, achieving complete fairness may be unfeasible in practice due to the complexity of diverse data sets. Therefore, a more practical framework for evaluating trade-offs between fairness and accuracy is proposed, enabling a balance between conflicting objectives. Experimental results show that this approach yields significant gains in fairness while maintaining a minimal impact on accuracy. The findings suggest that achieving a practical equilibrium between fairness and accuracy is a realistic and achievable goal. The research paves the way for future studies on evaluating and optimizing fairness in federated learning systems. Speech recognition models heavily rely on large datasets of annotated transcripts, which can be unaffordable for languages with limited resources. In this context, self-supervised pre-training emerges as a potential solution, enabling models to be trained on unlabelled speech and subsequently fine-tuned on specific tasks. However, pre-training's effectiveness depends on the quality of the unlabelled data, which can be compromised by factors such as speech noise and accent. In this research, we propose a new pre-training strategy that focuses on improving a model's ability to understand accent-specific pronunciation patterns in low-resource languages. Specifically, we develop a 'transcription-aware' self-supervised pre-training approach that trains speech models to recognize non-words and words in a text-to-speech style, utilizing an auxiliary transcript model to guide the model's learning. Our experiments demonstrate that this approach leads to significant improvements in speech recognition tasks, surpassing existing state-of-the-art results in low-resource languages such as Arabic and Hindi by as much as 21% relative. Moreover, our method proves to be adaptable across different domains, enabling models to achieve comparable performance even when trained on low-quality data from non-native speakers. In a study on communication among voters on a two-dimensional platform, I examine how
arguments evolve and how information spreads among participants. Initially, each voter holds a personal opinion, which they use to make statements. Their messages are then influenced by the responses from others, creating a dynamic process that unfolds over time. By tracking individual voter opinions, I discovered that social segregation occurs naturally, even when opinions are randomly distributed. Furthermore, I found that communication patterns tend to stabilize and become more segregated over time. Notably, the structure of these echo chambers depends on a range of factors, and I developed a model to describe them. This research has implications for understanding how information can be effectively disseminated in a society divided by different perspectives. Data structures like Bloom Filters, used for membership testing, rely on probabilistic algorithms that may lead to false positives - incorrect identification of a key not belonging to the set.  In this research, we've developed an approach to gauge the likelihood of false positives in a Bloom Filter, with the accuracy tied to the precision of a given threshold.  The proposed method involves generating random subsets from the population database and measuring false positive rates against these derived samples.  The process is repeated multiple times until the desired confidence level is achieved, at which point we can estimate the false positive probability.  To test our approach, we've created a web-based tool that allows users to set a confidence threshold and replicate the false positive estimation process.  Our tool not only offers the false positive probability but also provides an estimated count of actual keys that might be misidentified.  This innovative method of assessing false positive probabilities can be applied in various scenarios, with the source code available for review and adaptation. We propose a method for establishing the validity of a conjecture put forth by Leclerc that dual canonical bases of quantum group invariants at a generic root of unity are mutually dual. In support of this method, we demonstrate that it results in a bihomogeneous structure for dual canonical bases when applied to the $t$-deformation of the symplectic Lie algebra of $\mathfrak{so}_n$, provided $t$ is not a root of unity. As a consequence, this method yields a bihomogeneous structure for dual canonical bases of $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_{n})$ as well. The approach primarily relies on the fact that the $t$-deformation of the symplectic Lie algebra of $\mathfrak{so}_n$ can be viewed as a subalgebra within the $t$-deformation of the affine superalgebra $\hat{U}(\mathfrak{sp}_{2n}(A))$, where $A$ represents a commutative domain. The conjecture's validity for $\hat{U}(\mathfrak{sp}_{2n}(A))$ then follows from its established validity for $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_{2n+1})$. The conjecture's validity for $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_{n})$ subsequently follows from its validity for $\hat{U}(\mathfrak{sp}_{2n}(A))$. To achieve this, it's crucial to bridge the communication gap between humans' verbal expressions and robots' physical movements. However, this task is complex due to the inherent ambiguity of language. Collaborative filtering (CF) based recommender systems have become an integral part of our daily lives, yet they face a significant issue of popularity bias, causing users to interact with items in proportion to their promotion, which in turn hampers the discovery of novel content. This work delves into the problem of popularity bias by examining the underlying latent factors driving user-item interactions and proposes a new approach, latent factor bias reduction, aimed at mitigating the distortion of true user preferences by removing promotional influence from the latent factors. Our proposed method, which is model-agnostic and efficient, has been extensively evaluated on real-world datasets, resulting in a substantial improvement of up to 35% in the diversity-utility ratio. This outcome not only highlights the potential of this method in enhancing utility and diversity but also underscores the importance of unbiased recommendations in preserving user autonomy in the age of personalized systems. Predicting traffic accidents from surveillance footage is crucial for ensuring road safety.
Traditional methods employing video analysis techniques such as object detection, segmentation, and feature extraction are hindered by the scarcity of training data.
To address this issue, we present an innovative solution, called Attention-based Spatio-Temporal Transformer (ASTrans), for predicting traffic accidents from limited video data.
ASTrans is an end-to-end model that incorporates the Transformer architecture for predicting traffic accidents from surveillance footage.
It incorporates an attention mechanism to identify dynamic patterns in traffic accidents from limited video data.
We evaluate ASTrans on a public dataset and demonstrate its superior performance over existing models for accident prediction. Notably, ASTrans achieves a significant improvement of 10% in macro F1 score over the second-best approach. Moreover, it successfully predicts accidents from surveillance footage captured in less than 10 seconds, a duration that is more realistic in urban environments. This achievement showcases ASTrans's effectiveness in predicting traffic accidents from limited video data. The study of scientific publication networks has become increasingly significant in evaluating the credibility of researchers, with various centrality measures proposed to assess an author's influence within these networks. This paper employs the log-normal model to represent the population distribution of centrality measures and uses maximum likelihood estimation to fit the model using various sample sizes. Furthermore, the relationships between the log-normal model parameters and the widely used position-based measures (e.g., eigencentrality, betweenness centrality, degree centrality) are examined. Interestingly, the study reveals a strong correlation between degree centrality and the h-index, indicating a potential alternative to the h-index as a more efficient measure of researcher reputation. Additionally, the study compares the performance of the log-normal model to other popular models, such as the Zipf's r-power law and the Strauss-Moorcroft model, under different conditions and network types. The results show that the log-normal model outperforms its competitors in certain scenarios, highlighting its potential as a versatile and efficient tool for analyzing scientific publication networks. Ultimately, the study suggests that the log-normal model can be a valuable asset in evaluating researcher reputation and network centrality measures. This study introduces the first adaptive moment descent (MDD) algorithm, 
PMD-PD, for constrained non-convex optimization problems, ensuring both 
primal and dual feasibility. A novel constraint enforcement method is developed 
using a penalty and proximal update process to enforce dual feasibility. A 
derivative-free algorithm, PMD-SQN, is also proposed for unconstrained non-convex 
optimization, utilizing quadratic adjustments to approximate gradients. 
Convergence rates are analytically demonstrated for both PMD-PD and PMD-SQN 
algorithms, showing the optimality gap and constraint violations decrease at a 
cubic rate. Experimental results confirm the algorithms' cubic convergence, 
outperforming existing methods in non-convex optimization tasks. Additionally, 
applications in deep neural network training demonstrate PMD-PD's ability to

A novel unsupervised optical flow learning approach, known as SMURF, integrates a motion layer and a residual motion layer to enhance the extraction of motion information. The residual term in this framework is designed to compensate for the motion layer's limitations by incorporating a multi-layer perceptron that predicts the residual between a frame and its corresponding flow-deformed frame. Through a self-supervised learning process, SMURF optimizes the motion layer and residual term such that the predicted residual approaches zero. The framework's ability to learn a residual term is made possible by utilizing a residual loss term that encourages the predicted residual to match the actual residual. This could enable the creation of dynamic, fault-tolerant networks that can adapt to and recover from physical damage. Additionally, this research explores ways to mitigate these privacy risks, such as implementing standardized protocols, protecting device interoperability, and adhering to standardization, by analyzing an IoT system that incorporates energy meters within a building that uses a smart gateway connected to the cloud via cellular networks, ensuring privacy is maintained throughout the ecosystem. A comprehensive review of case studies, standards, and legislation reveals that while guidelines for smart metering and IoT are available, there is still a need for standardization, particularly in the energy metering field to ensure data security and protection. This research aims to provide a comprehensive understanding of IoT data, smart building energy metering devices, and the laws governing data usage to inform future IoT development and research. Ultimately, this research aims to contribute to the development of a unified IoT ecosystem that prioritizes user privacy and security. It also aims to provide a foundation for future research in IoT data security and protection. This paper introduces a novel concept, image restoration potential (IRP), designed to evaluate the suitability of noise reference images for noise prediction in image restoration. The proposed approach utilizes noise-free target images and noise reference images to develop a predictive model, and it is predicted that this model can generalize to unknown noise environments. The predicted noise reference image restoration potential (NRIP) is defined as the image similarity between the noise reference image and the noise-polluted target image. A deep learning-based method, called NRIP-guided image restoration (NIR), is developed to restore images using the noise-polluted target image as input. Experimental results demonstrate that NIR outperforms other state-of-the-art methods in image restoration, and NRIP effectively assesses the predictive capability of noise reference images. We utilize ViLM to extract video representations by first generating text tokens from video inputs and then obtaining embeddings from the model's pre-trained language components. Moreover, our findings indicate that well-trained language models can effectively transfer knowledge between domains, resulting in improved performance on out-of-distribution video datasets. Music streaming platforms provide three main ways to access content: searching, browsing through categories, and recommended lists. This study examines how users rely on these modes interactively, particularly comparing search and playback subscription among users of Spotify, the most popular music streaming platform. A comprehensive analysis was conducted based on 675,000 users' streaming and search activity over a period of 81 days, employing a survival analysis that takes into account subscription patterns. The research found that users who frequently used search are more likely to subscribe to premium playback, particularly if they made fewer searches during their current session. Conversely, the likelihood of subscribing decreases as users make more searches within a session. The research also found that users who frequently browse categories are less likely to subscribe to premium playback, indicating a substitution effect between categories and paid playback. The results have significant implications for music streaming platforms, suggesting opportunities to tailor personalized experiences and promotional strategies tailored to individual user interactions. Researchers have previously utilized either parametric or non-parametric multiple imputation, but an alternative non-parametric approach, utilizing a data-driven method to estimate response distributions based on observed data, has been underutilized. This study presents findings on the efficacy of one such data-driven method, specifically the k-nearest neighbors method, compared to parametric MI and a widely used non-parametric approach, 2.5-Dice. Experimental results indicate that the k-nearest neighbors method performs comparably to the other methods when the data is normally distributed, but it offers superior results in scenarios with non-normal data. This method's effectiveness is further demonstrated by its ability to outperform other methods in certain non-parametric simulations. Additionally, the study reveals that the k-nearest neighbors method achieves comparable performance to MI in certain scenarios. These findings suggest that this method could be a viable alternative to MI in certain applications involving selective missingness. A Python-based implementation of the k-nearest neighbors method is provided to facilitate future research. This study's results have significant implications for researchers in statistics and data science. A related R package, knnim, is publicly available and offers an efficient solution for handling selective missing data in various data analysis tasks. In contrast, our proposed metric, Integrated Fairness Measure (IFM), continuously updates its fairness awareness by integrating the probability distribution of the data space as it's explored. We demonstrate that IFM yields more accurate assessments of fairness and outperforms existing methods, particularly in scenarios where data is sampled from a distribution different from the initial assumption. IFM also offers a unified framework for handling various fairness constraints, showcasing its effectiveness in a series of experiments. A novel approach unifies all gauge symmetries encountered in the Standard Model and beyond. This unification, achieved through a tensor product of the gauge group, results in a larger, non-Abelian Lie group that retains elements of the original gauge group. When applied to the Standard Model, the resulting unification yields a simple, four-dimensional Lie group, $\mathrm{G}_{4}$. The same method can be used to unify the Standard Model's gauge symmetries with gravity, producing an extended Lie group, $\mathrm{G}_{4}^{g}$. Furthermore, the unification of all gauge symmetries, including gravity, yields an even larger Lie group, $\mathrm{G}_{8}$, whose representation includes the original gauge group. Using this extended Lie group, the action for a Dirac fermion is formulated, and the resulting Dirac equation is solved to obtain a mass-dependent wave function. The resulting mass spectrum is determined, and the prediction for the Yukawa coupling, $α_{e}$, is calculated. The model's predictions for $α_{e}(m_{t})$ and $α_{e}(m_{e})$ align with observed values, and the model's implications for the Yukawa couplings of quarks and leptons are also explored. We introduce the Simplified Laplace Approximation (SLAP) method for efficiently computing the posterior distribution of Bayesian hierarchical models. SLAP yields an accurate approximation of the posterior mean under minimal assumptions, utilizing a single optimization step. In contrast, Laplace approximation methods necessitate iterative adjustments of local approximations. While the original Laplace method was proven to be computationally efficient due to its closed-form solution for Gaussian models, its extension to hierarchical models introduced significant computational hurdles. SLAP sidesteps these challenges by separately estimating parameters in two distinct stages: first, the linear parameters, followed by the nonlinear parameters. SLAP's efficiency stems from the analytical solution for linear parameters, allowing for fast computation via closed-form expressions. In practice, SLAP outperforms other approximation methods by achieving the same efficiency as the exact solution, while reducing computational time to mere milliseconds for large datasets. We demonstrate SLAP's applicability through various examples, including linear mixed models, Gaussian processes, and hierarchical matrix tensor factorization. Our research focuses on the thermodynamic and dynamic changes within a model consisting of Ising spins on a two-dimensional pyrochlore lattice. This work provides a detailed examination of the impact of planarity on the valence bond solid and superfluid phases, and sheds light on the underlying mechanisms governing the behavior of frustrated spin systems. By utilizing DINO, researchers and practitioners can quickly experiment with new model variations, test their performance on established benchmarks, and share their findings with the community. This approach enables the development of more robust and generalizable models, and accelerates progress in areas such as domain generalization and continuous learning. Our analysis centers on a system where resources are distributed according to utility functions that define each agent's individual preferences. We draw inspiration from existing research on fair division among agents, yet acknowledge its limitations due to the complexity of modeling intricate agent interactions. To address these constraints, we propose a novel approach based on a deep reinforcement learning method that enables the autonomous definition of utility functions by the agents themselves. This approach allows agents to autonomously develop their utility functions, which are then utilized to determine the optimal resource distribution among them. We demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed deep reinforcement learning-based technique in achieving improved resource allocation outcomes compared to existing methods. Furthermore, we examine the potential biases that may arise in the learned utility functions, particularly in situations where resources are allocated to agents with varying levels of need. To mitigate these biases, we also investigate the incorporation of a fairness penalty term into the utility functions. Our results demonstrate the feasibility of our proposed approach in designing more equitable resource distribution algorithms. Comprehensive numerical experiments are conducted to validate the performance of our approach. Additionally, we provide a theoretical analysis of our proposed algorithm to gain deeper insights into its properties. This analysis is further substantiated through experiments and visualizations. Finally, we explore the potential applications of our approach in real-world scenarios through a practical case study involving the allocation of data resources in a distributed data management system. The results of our research provide a comprehensive understanding of the $\frac{5}{3}$ state, including its microscopic structure and macroscopic properties. The results of our research have the potential to unlock new insights into the behavior of quantum Hall liquids and charge density waves, as well as the development of novel technologies based on these states. Ultimately, the study of the $\frac{5}{3}$ state, a complex and multifaceted system, provides a unique opportunity to integrate our understanding of the physics of charge density waves, quantum Hall liquids, and superconductivity into a unified picture. We present an improved version of the averaged Langevin Monte Carlo algorithm, specifically tailored for high-dimensional target distributions. By leveraging the underlying gradient properties of the potential function, we establish conditions for mixing times and prove that it can sample from a diverse set of target distributions, as long as the potential function has a Lipschitz gradient. Notably, our method can effectively sample from a Gibbs distribution over a set of discrete configurations, given that the potential energy function is associated with these configurations. Experimental results demonstrate the practical utility of this modified algorithm, even in scenarios where the gradient of the potential function is not well-defined in an infinitesimal sense. However, this modification incurs a slight increase in step size, resulting in a more efficient algorithm, compared to its traditional counterpart. Notably, we also show that the mixing time of this modified algorithm is directly proportional to the inverse of the number of discrete configurations, allowing it to sample from a Gibbs distribution over these states. As an additional benefit, we establish a bound on the mixing time of this modified algorithm, specifically $O(d\log(n))$, where $d$ represents the dimension of the space and $n$ denotes the number of discrete configurations, for a target distribution with a potential function that is $1$-strongly convex and has a Lipschitz gradient. Our results are complemented by numerical experiments that highlight the effectiveness of this modified algorithm in comparison to its traditional counterpart. For edge connectivity, we develop a randomized algorithm that can determine the minimum edge cut $k$ in $O(m\alpha^2+k\log n)$ time, achieving a constant error probability, where $\alpha = O(m/n)$. This result bridges the gap between existing algorithms and establishes a new benchmark for randomized edge connectivity.

Deterministically, we improve the time complexity for edge connectivity from $O(m\alpha^2\log m +k\log^3 m)$ to $O(m\alpha^2+k\alpha\log m)$. This new bound highlights a linear improvement over the previous determinant-based approach.

For vertex connectivity, we develop a deterministic algorithm that can identify the minimum vertex cut size $\kappa(G)$ in $O(m\kappa\log m+n\kappa\log n)$ time, achieving a constant error probability. This result expands upon existing algorithms that can determine $\kappa(G)$ in $O(m\kappa\log m +k\log^3 m)$ time.

By leveraging this construction, we can optimize the number of queries required to determine edge and vertex connectivity. The goal of disentangled representation learning is to extract independent factors from data, enabling flexible image control. However, current methods primarily focus on quantitative disentanglement metrics and qualitative demonstrations, failing to fully capture the challenges of controlling complex images. To bridge this gap, our research proposes a new evaluation metric that assesses the quality of controllable representations in image synthesis tasks. This metric examines the ability to identify and independently control various image features, including textures, colors, and subjects. By utilizing this metric to evaluate different techniques, such as color, texture, and subject control, as well as their integration, we found that existing disentanglement approaches fall short in various scenarios, and specifically in text-to-image synthesis tasks. To address this limitation, we introduced the Disentangle and Condition Image Generator (D-CIG) framework, which integrates a disentanglement module with a GAN to generate high-quality images. By incorporating a conditional layer that utilizes disentangled factors, D-CIG produces more accurate and visually appealing results. Experiments conducted on various datasets demonstrate that D-CIG outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in both disentanglement and image generation tasks. Furthermore, the proposed evaluation metric provides a more comprehensive understanding of the disentanglement process. A breakthrough approach in 3D scene reconstruction, Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF), has a major limitation in real-world applications where untrained users capture dynamic scenes with moving objects. Current methods fail to handle such scenarios due to a lack of consistent sampling over time. To address this, we introduce a novel technique, Time Neural Radiance Fields (TNRF), which extends NeRF to capture complex, dynamic scenes with moving objects by learning a joint 3D scene representation across time. This is achieved through a proposed neural network architecture that enables efficient training with minimal scene knowledge. Furthermore, we develop a novel time-varying optimization approach to ensure consistent spatial consistency across different time points. Leveraging the spatial-temporal structure of the scene, TNRF can efficiently reconstruct and render dynamic scenes with moving objects, achieving high-quality results even with casual, untrained captures. To demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, we conduct extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world scenes, resulting in superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art methods. The field of Explainable AI (XAI) has made significant strides in recent years, with a focus on developing post-hoc methods to explain the decisions of complex algorithms. These methods can be categorized into two distinct approaches, depending on the level of access available to the explanation algorithm. With some algorithms, known as black-box models, access is restricted and explanations must be derived from input and output data alone, often through data-driven methods. In contrast, other algorithms, such as white-box models, provide direct access to internal workings and explanations can be generated through more versatile means. This paper will examine recent advancements in XAI, with a focus on black-box models, to determine the suitability of these methods for evaluating the explanatory power of complex algorithms. Through a comprehensive review of these methods, we will highlight their benefits and limitations, and provide guidance on their effective use. Finally, we will examine the current state of the field and identify areas for future research. With advancements in XAI, we are increasingly able to understand the inner workings of complex algorithms, and with continued innovation, we may soon possess the tools necessary to ensure that AI systems are transparent, trustworthy, and ultimately human-aware. However, this requires a concerted effort from the academic and industrial research communities to develop and refine these tools, with a focus on developing practical solutions that can be applied in real-world scenarios. This may necessitate the development of novel methods that can be integrated into existing AI systems with minimal disruption. Ultimately, the success of XAI will depend on our ability to provide actionable insights that can be used by AI practitioners to build more trustworthy and explainable systems. With the right approach, we may soon possess the tools necessary to address the pressing challenges facing our world and create a brighter future for all. The field of cybersecurity is heavily reliant on the evaluation and comparison of different methods to combat specific threats, making high-quality research data sets with reproducible results essential.  However, given the complexity of cyberattacks, identifying and documenting a comprehensive dataset is an extremely time-consuming task.  To address this issue, we introduce CyDrone, a large dataset containing over 3000 authentic samples of malicious activity related to drone-based attacks, extracted directly from the real-world IoT network of the EDISON project.  By leveraging existing IoT devices, we ensure the well-documented nature and validity of CyDrone, making it possible to effectively train deep learning models for accurate cybersecurity assessments.  To demonstrate the value of this dataset, we conduct an in-depth analysis of malicious behavior using deep learning models, showcasing their effectiveness in identifying high-risk behavior patterns.  Furthermore, we also present a new deep learning architecture that leverages attention mechanisms to identify critical network elements and detect potential security threats.  By making CyDrone publicly available, we aim to promote further research and cross-validation in the field of cybersecurity.  The dataset is accessible at https://github.com/ai4hr/CyDrone. Notably, MoNArch achieves state-of-the-art performance on the NuScenes dataset under the IoU-based metric. The architecture's design allows for efficient inference, requiring only a single forward pass even in real-time settings. Additionally, MoNArch's design enables a straightforward integration of future context, making it a suitable foundation for developing advanced, architecture-agnostic, and generalizable monocular 3D object tracking and multi-object detection techniques. We analyze a nonlinear Schrödinger equation influenced by a fractional Laplacian, 
with singular nonlocal terms and nonconstant positive potentials 
defined on the entire real line. The paper's goal is to establish the existence 
of positive, decreasing ground states when the nonlinear function has a critical exponent 
and exhibits subcritical, critical, or slightly supercritical properties. To achieve this, 
we introduce an equivalent problem defined in a higher dimensional Euclidean space 
and utilize a technique that involves constructing a suitable positive ground state 
for this transformed problem. Leveraging the fractional Hardy-Littlewood inequality 
and a specific cut-off strategy, we then demonstrate the existence of positive, 
decreasing ground states for the original problem. Our findings are also accompanied 
by regularity results and, as a byproduct, we also establish the nonexistence 
of positive, increasing ground states within the supercritical regime. 
Furthermore, we also demonstrate that positive, decreasing ground states can be 
constructed for a modified, singular Schrödinger equation involving fractional 
Lapllacian with singular terms and nonconstant positive potentials. This modified 
problem is defined on the entire real line. Our approach relies on 
utilizing a cut-off strategy and a technique similar to the one employed 
in our previous analysis. We also establish regularity results and a specific 
form of decay for the positive, decreasing ground states associated with this 
modified problem. We accomplish this by employing a specific cut-off strategy 
and a technique similar to the one employed in our previous analysis. Our approach 
is also shown to be applicable to higher dimensional Euclidean spaces. 
The paper's final section includes a specific example illustrating the application 
of our findings to the modified, singular Schrödinger equation involving 
fractional Laplacian with singular terms and nonconstant positive potentials.

We demonstrate that for a coherent analytic sheaf of pure dimension, the Chern class of its underlying fundamental cycle coincides with the Chern class of a related sheaf of forms equipped with $(1,0)$-connections, assuming the connection is flat. Furthermore, this theorem can be applied to derive novel topological inequalities by combining established inequalities related to vanishing and cohomology. Our method involves a two-stage process where the annotation information of one dataset is adapted to match another, allowing datasets to supplement one another's coverage. In this study, we introduce an efficient policy learning algorithm tailored for non-stationary environments, referred to as VINE. VINE is derived from the soft actor-critic algorithm and optimized with the incorporation of an innovation statistic that signifies the deviation of the current state from its stationary distribution. Building upon this, we developed VINE-GAE, a variant of the actor-critic method that utilizes the generalized advantage estimate, providing a more accurate calculation of the innovation statistic. The performance of VINE and VINE-GAE is evaluated in a non-stationary environment setting and found to outshine soft actor-critic algorithms in multiple testing scenarios. Our research contributes to the development of more robust model explanations, enabling better decision-making and more reliable AI systems. The findings are validated through a comparison with alternative encryption techniques. Defending computer networks against sophisticated cyber-attacks is an intricate task. 
Effective countermeasures must strike a balance between being able to detect and respond to both anticipated and unforeseen threats, and not to disrupt the functioning of monitored systems or misidentify legitimate users and network elements. 
This requirement creates a significant challenge due to the inherent uncertainty associated with complex cyber security scenarios and the limited visibility into potential threats, making it difficult to anticipate the actions of an adversary. 
To address these difficulties, this research proposes an innovative approach, referred to as Dynamic Threat Defense (DTD), which leverages a probabilistic reasoning framework, referred to as Dynamic Probabilistic Reasoning, to create an adaptive threat defence solution. 
This framework enables a real-time assessment of network activity and allows for the identification of potential threats, along with the development of an automated defence strategy. 
A key component of DTD is its ability to utilize a probabilistic model of network activity, referred to as Dynamic Bayesian Networks, to reason about complex cyber security scenarios in real-time. 
This model is updated dynamically, taking into account network activity and network alerts, to provide a unified and coherent understanding of the network. 
In addition, this research proposes a novel algorithm, referred to as the Dynamic Probabilistic Reasoning algorithm, to enable the adaptive defence strategy. 
This algorithm utilizes the insights gained from the probabilistic model to provide a real-time defence strategy that is tailored to the specific network scenario. 
A proof of concept implementation of the DTD solution was developed using Python, demonstrating its effectiveness in real-world scenarios. 
This paper presents a comprehensive overview of the DTD solution, along with the results of experiments conducted to evaluate its effectiveness. 
A comparative analysis of the performance of the DTD solution against other leading cyber security solutions is also provided, highlighting its potential to provide adaptive threat defence. 
Finally, this research highlights the key advantages and potential applications of the DTD solution, along with potential areas for future research into dynamic threat defence solutions.

Structural seismic interpretation relies heavily on estimating subsurface properties like depth and deformation to understand complex geological formations. While deep learning has shown promise in automating this process, the spatial relationships among these attributes are often overlooked. Through both synthetic and field data experiments, the approach has demonstrated improved accuracy in concurrent estimation tasks. This is exemplified by a 130 km$^2$ North Sea seismic dataset, where the spatially-aware approach outperformed its non-spatial counterpart in estimating depths and velocities. This research marks the first attempt to simultaneously estimate multiple subsurface properties while considering their spatial relationships. The task of open set recognition involves distinguishing between known (target) classes and unknown classes in a machine learning context. We propose a novel approach to open set recognition, utilising the concept of adversarial training to develop a classifier that responds to input based on the available classes. The results suggest that our method effectively addresses the open set problem while maintaining high accuracy for in-distribution classes. Furthermore, our approach allows for efficient training without the need for additional loss functions or network components, making it a computationally feasible solution. To our knowledge, this is the first time adversarial training has been applied to open set recognition, and our method demonstrates promising performance in this domain. This paper introduces a Lexical Conceptual Structure-based system that conceptualizes and structures meanings associated with social engineering behaviors. By representing and modeling specific instances of social engineering, it aims to enhance automatic detection through lexicographic channels. The meaningful units and relations that make up Lexical Conceptual Structure are used to encode the essential components and interactions of social engineering, covering concepts like contact, communication, manipulation, and establishment of relationships. Additionally, the paper explores instances of social engineering, such as phishing, and represents their constituent components within the framework of Lexical Conceptual Structure. The resulting representation enables the automatic recognition and identification of such behaviors, and the paper outlines key technical considerations regarding the formalization. Finally, potential applications of the system are identified, along with the challenges that must be addressed in order to realize its full potential. The advantages of using Lexical Conceptual Structure for modeling and engineering are highlighted, and the paper concludes by exploring its broader implications for the field of automatic threat detection. The accompanying technical appendix provides detailed explanations of the technical aspects underlying the system. Three appendices are included: (1) a detailed examination of the technical feasibility of the approach, (2) a discussion of the role played by Lexical Conceptual Structure in social engineering modeling, and (3) an analysis of the implications for the automatic detection of social engineering, including phishing. Estimating light field depth is crucial for many computer vision applications, but existing deep learning methods are often complex, slow, and unreliable due to their reliance on extensive datasets or overfitting. To address these limitations, this research proposes a novel, accurate light field depth estimation approach that utilizes a streamlined cost constructor based on a lightweight network, achieving superior performance without compromising efficiency. By leveraging a single-cost constructor design, this model surpasses state-of-the-art methods on synthetic and real-world datasets, with results that are not only more precise but also less prone to inaccuracies. To further enhance its adaptability, this model incorporates a method for selecting the most relevant views, effectively mitigating the impact of occlusions. Experimental results confirm the effectiveness of the proposed method, with running times of less than a second on entire light fields and impressive accuracy metrics, including an L1 error of 0.0460 and a R-squared value of 0.9742 on the MPI light fields dataset.
